anabaptist-mennonite-peace-church.in_a_sentence: Churches that baptise only people old enough to ask for it, read the Sermon on the Mount as a way of life rather than an ideal, and refuse to carry a weapon. Mennonites, Hutterites and the Amish all belong here.
what_marks_it_out: The founding argument was about baptism, and it has never stopped being the centre of the thing. In January 1525, in a private house in Zurich, a handful of young men baptised one another as adults, having decided that a baby cannot make the promise baptism asks for. Their opponents called them Anabaptists, which means rebaptisers. It was not a nickname. It was a criminal charge.

The second mark is nonresistance: the refusal to use force, including in war, in self-defence and in the courts. The Schleitheim Confession of 1527 works through it in its sixth article, on the sword. Anabaptists read the instruction not to resist an evildoer (Matthew 5:39) as an order given to the church, meant to be obeyed now, rather than as an ideal for a better world. Most of the other distinctives follow from taking the Sermon on the Mount as instructions.

On grace the sketch puts them firmly on the synergist side, where God’s grace comes first and the person freely cooperates with it. Anabaptists rarely argue about predestination at all. Their weight falls on what happens after conversion: a faith you can watch someone live, inside a congregation that holds its members to it.

The rest follows the same instinct. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance of Christ’s death and a sign that the congregation is one body, not a change in the bread; many churches wash one another’s feet at the same service, which the Dordrecht Confession of 1632 treats as an ordinance in its own right. Scripture stands alone above every creed, but it is read out and argued over by the gathered congregation rather than settled by a scholar. Worship is plain, and Mennonites are known for unaccompanied four-part singing.

did_you_know.text: Felix Manz, one of the men in that Zurich house, was drowned in the river Limmat on 5 January 1527. The council had ruled the year before that rebaptisers should be put to death by drowning. The punishment was chosen to mock what they had done.
did_you_know.source: Zurich council edict of 7 March 1526; Manz executed 5 January 1527, the first Anabaptist martyred by Protestant authorities.

did_you_know.text: On 23 April 1529 the Diet of Speyer made rebaptism a capital offence across the whole Holy Roman Empire, with Catholic and Lutheran princes voting the same way. Four days earlier the same diet had produced the formal protest that gave Protestants their name.
did_you_know.source: Imperial mandate of 23 April 1529, Diet of Speyer; the Protestation at Speyer, 19 April 1529.

did_you_know.text: The Amish are Mennonites who left in 1693. Jakob Ammann, an elder in Switzerland, wanted members under discipline shunned in daily life; Hans Reist and the elders of the Emmental did not, and the argument split the Swiss Brethren in two.
did_you_know.source: The Amish Division, 1693, over Meidung (shunning); Ammann and Reist.

anabaptist-mennonite-peace-church.family: The radical wing of the Reformation. It began in Zurich in 1525 among men who had been Zwingli’s own students and concluded that he had stopped half way. Mennonites take their name from Menno Simons, a Dutch priest who joined them in 1536 and spent the rest of his life gathering scattered survivors. Hutterites, the Amish, the Brethren in Christ and the Bruderhof all grew from the same root. Quakers are not descended from them, but arrive at much the same place on peace.

read.placed_from: Schleitheim Confession (1527) 1-4; Dordrecht Confession (1632) 7-9; Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995) 11-12.

open.title: The Schleitheim Confession (1527)
open.note: Seven short articles, agreed in a Swiss village two years after the first rebaptism. Article 1 is baptism, article 4 separation from the world, article 6 the sword.

open.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995)
open.note: Twenty-four articles, and the working confession of North American Mennonites today. Article 11 is baptism; article 22 is peace, justice and nonresistance.

anglican-broad.in_a_sentence: The Church of England and the churches grown from it, which kept bishops, a prayer book and the church year at the Reformation. Its settlement was built to hold people who disagree.
what_marks_it_out: Anglicans are marked out more by how they pray than by what they argue. The Book of Common Prayer, largely Thomas Cranmer’s work, sets the words for morning and evening prayer, communion, baptism, marriage and burial, and the 1662 edition is still the Church of England’s legal standard of doctrine. A visitor knows roughly what will happen before it happens, and so does the vicar.

On communion the sketch places Anglicans firmly at the sacramental end. Article XXVIII of the Thirty-Nine Articles rejects transubstantiation, the teaching that the bread and wine stop being bread and wine, as “repugnant to the plain words of Scripture”, and in the very next breath says the body of Christ is “given, taken, and eaten, in the Supper, only after an heavenly and spiritual manner”. Both halves are meant.

On grace the map names no position, and that is an honest reading rather than a gap. Article XVII teaches predestination to life, which is the idea that God chose His people before the world began, and then says nothing whatever about the other half of the question. The silence was deliberate. Calvinists and Arminians have both signed the Articles in good conscience for four centuries.

Scripture comes first: Article VI says Holy Scripture “containeth all things necessary to salvation”, so nothing that cannot be read there or proved from it may be required of anyone as an article of belief. But the creeds, the early councils and the prayer book stay in daily use, which puts Anglicans on the Scripture-first side without pushing them to the pole. The word broad in the name is doing real work: Anglo-Catholics, evangelicals and a liberal middle all live inside one structure, and broad church has been an English term for exactly that willingness since the nineteenth century.

did_you_know.text: When Elizabeth I’s prayer book appeared in 1559, the words said as the bread is given joined the Catholic-sounding line of 1549, “The body of our Lord Jesus Christ”, to the Protestant-sounding line of 1552, “Take and eat this in remembrance”. Nobody chose. Both were printed, and both are still said today.
did_you_know.source: Book of Common Prayer 1559, words of administration, combining the 1549 and 1552 forms; retained in 1662.

did_you_know.text: There were forty-two Articles before there were thirty-nine. Cranmer’s set of 1553 was cut down under Elizabeth I and given its final form in 1571, which is the text clergy still assent to.
did_you_know.source: Forty-Two Articles (1553); Thirty-Nine Articles, final form 1571.

anglican-broad.family: A Reformation church inside a pre-Reformation body. The English church broke with Rome under Henry VIII in the 1530s and was made Protestant in doctrine under Edward VI and Elizabeth I, but kept its bishops, its cathedrals and its parishes whole. The Anglican Communion today runs from the Church of England to the Episcopal Church in the United States, the Church of Nigeria and dozens more. Methodists are the closest relatives of all: John Wesley was an Anglican priest and died one.

read.placed_from: Thirty-Nine Articles VI, VIII, XVII, XX, XXI, XXV, XXVII, XXVIII; Book of Common Prayer 1662, the calendar and the collects.

open.title: The Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion (1571)
open.note: A few pages, free online, and each article a paragraph. VI is Scripture, XVII predestination, XXVIII the Lord’s Supper.

open.title: The Book of Common Prayer (1662)
open.note: Readable straight through, and still the doctrinal standard. The collects are the short set prayers, one for each Sunday of the year.

bible-church-independent-dispensational.in_a_sentence: Independent congregations built around verse-by-verse Bible teaching, which keep Israel and the church distinct as two peoples of God. Most expect Christ to take the church home before the world’s last troubles.
what_marks_it_out: Start with the word. A dispensation is a stretch of history in which God deals with people under a particular arrangement, and dispensationalists read the Bible as a sequence of them. But the load-bearing claim is not the number of periods. It is the distinction: Israel is Israel and the church is the church, and the promises of land and throne made to Israel will be kept to Israel rather than quietly transferred to the church. Charles Ryrie, who taught at Dallas, named three things a dispensationalist must hold: that distinction, a consistently literal reading of prophecy, and God’s own glory rather than salvation as the point of history.

The church is expected to be taken up to meet Christ in the air before the tribulation, the period of judgement described in Revelation, with the visible return following afterwards. This is the rapture that most people have heard of even if they have never heard the word dispensational, and it is why these churches sit at the far end of the Israel-and-the-church axis.

On grace the map names no position here, and the founding documents show why. These churches are largely Calvinist on election and on the believer’s security, but they will not say Christ died only for the chosen: the Dallas statement says He “gave His life as a ransom for all”. Holding four of Calvinism’s five points leaves you sitting on the line rather than on one side of it.

Everything else follows one instinct, which is that the text is enough. The sermon is the service, and it walks through a book of the Bible a paragraph at a time. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance, kept as often as the congregation decides. No bishop, synod or denomination stands over the elders, which is what independent means on the sign outside. And the spectacular gifts, tongues and prophecy and healing, are held to have belonged to the years when the apostles were laying the church’s foundation and finished with it.

did_you_know.text: Dispensationalism reached ordinary readers through a Bible rather than a book. C. I. Scofield’s reference Bible, published by Oxford University Press in 1909, printed the whole scheme in the margin beside the text. For two generations of American Christians the notes and the Scripture were read as one page.
did_you_know.source: Scofield Reference Bible, Oxford University Press, 1909. Its seven dispensations: Innocence, Conscience, Human Government, Promise, Law, Grace, Kingdom.

did_you_know.text: Dallas Theological Seminary, founded in 1924 by Lewis Sperry Chafer, is where most of this movement’s pastors trace their teaching. Its own doctrinal statement is more restrained than the famous charts: it treats three dispensations at length, the Mosaic Law, the present age of grace, and the millennial kingdom still to come.
did_you_know.source: Dallas Theological Seminary doctrinal statement, Article V; seminary founded 1924.

bible-church-independent-dispensational.family: The independent Bible church grew out of the Bible and prophecy conferences of the late nineteenth century, and behind those stands John Nelson Darby, an Irish curate who left the Church of Ireland for the Plymouth Brethren in the 1820s and worked the system out on long preaching tours of North America. From there it spread far beyond the churches that carry the label: Baptists, Calvary Chapel and much of American evangelicalism absorbed the rapture and the charts without ever taking the name.

read.placed_from: Dallas Theological Seminary doctrinal statement, Articles III-V and XVIII-XX; Ryrie, Dispensationalism; Chafer, Systematic Theology IV.

open.title: The Dallas Theological Seminary doctrinal statement
open.note: Short, numbered and online. Article V is the dispensations, XIII the church as distinct from Israel, XVIII the rapture.

open.title: Charles Ryrie, Dispensationalism
open.note: The movement explaining itself to its critics, including the three marks it says are essential to the system.

calvary-chapel.in_a_sentence: A fellowship of churches begun in California in 1965, known for teaching straight through the Bible book by book. It stands on purpose between fundamentalist and Pentecostal habits.
what_marks_it_out: The teaching method is the identity. A Calvary Chapel pastor starts at Genesis 1 and works to Revelation 22, a passage at a time, over years, rather than choosing a topic each week. Nothing is skipped because it is awkward. Chuck Smith, who began the whole thing in Costa Mesa, taught through the entire Bible from the pulpit and the recordings are still in use.

On the gifts of the Holy Spirit this tradition is misread constantly. Calvary Chapel believes every gift is still given today, tongues and prophecy and healing included. It also holds that the main Sunday service is not where they belong, reading Paul’s instructions about order in 1 Corinthians 14 strictly, and puts them in separate meetings afterwards. Smith described the position as middle ground: fundamentalism, he thought, had gone rigid and shut the gifts down, while Pentecostalism had let enthusiasm crowd out the teaching of the text.

On grace the map names nothing, and here the silence is a decision rather than a gap. Calvary Chapel accepts most of Calvinism and refuses two pieces of it: that Christ died only for the chosen, and that God’s call cannot be resisted by anyone who wants to resist it. Smith wrote a small book to explain why he would not take either label. Congregations contain both sorts of people and are meant to.

The last three readings all come out at the far end. Smith taught that Christ will take the church home before the tribulation and preached it hard. Worship is a band, an open Bible and no robes. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance. And no denominational office tells any congregation what to preach: churches associate voluntarily and keep their own pastor’s authority.

did_you_know.text: Modern worship music has a birthday and an address. Maranatha! Music began in 1971 as Calvary Chapel’s own label, so that the folk-rock songs its young converts were writing could be recorded. Its first album was The Everlastin’ Living Jesus Music Concert.
did_you_know.source: Maranatha! Music, founded 1971 by Chuck Smith as the house label of Calvary Chapel Costa Mesa; debut album 1971.

did_you_know.text: The Vineyard churches are Calvary Chapel’s most famous departure. John Wimber’s congregation in Yorba Linda separated in 1982, over how freely the gifts of the Holy Spirit should be used in a Sunday service, and became the flagship of a new movement.
did_you_know.source: Calvary Chapel Yorba Linda separated in 1982 and became Anaheim Vineyard under John Wimber.

calvary-chapel.family: A child of the Jesus People revival. Chuck Smith took over a tiny church in Costa Mesa, California, in 1965, and within a few years it had filled with the young converts of the Jesus movement. Doctrinally it stands close to the independent Bible churches, and shares their rapture and their verse-by-verse habit; where it parts from them is on the gifts, which it keeps. On the other side, the Vineyard and much of the charismatic world came out of Calvary Chapel rather than the reverse.

read.placed_from: Calvary Chapel Distinctives (Chuck Smith); Calvary Chapel Association Statement of Faith.

open.title: Chuck Smith, Calvary Chapel Distinctives
open.note: Short, and the movement in its founder’s own voice: why verse by verse, why the gifts, why not a denomination.

open.title: The Calvary Chapel Association Statement of Faith
open.note: Worth reading for what it settles and what it refuses to settle.

catholic-roman-and-eastern.in_a_sentence: The largest body of Christians on earth, governed from Rome, holding that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist. Scripture here is read inside the church’s living tradition, never apart from it.
what_marks_it_out: Catholics do not set Scripture against tradition. They deny that the question makes sense. Dei Verbum, the Second Vatican Council’s document on revelation, says Scripture and tradition flow from the same divine wellspring, and that the job of interpreting them authentically belongs to the church’s teaching office. So a Catholic meeting a hard passage asks what the church has understood it to mean, and experiences that as the way the Bible is heard rather than as a fence around it.

At Mass the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. The word for it is transubstantiation: what the elements look like, taste like and are chemically stays the same, what they are does not. Trent said so in 1551 and the Catechism repeats it at paragraphs 1374 to 1376. This is the deepest sacramental position on the map, and everything else in a Catholic church is arranged around the altar where it happens.

On grace the sketch surprises people by leaning to the cooperating side, so it is worth being exact. Catholic teaching is emphatic that nothing whatever is earned at the start: the Catechism calls grace the free and undeserved help God gives us, and Trent taught that justification begins with grace that runs ahead of anything a person does. But Trent also condemned the idea that the human will is merely passive and cannot refuse its consent, and refusal is precisely what this axis measures. God moves first, and the person can still say no.

Worship is liturgical at the deepest end: a fixed order, a calendar running from Advent round to Christ the King, and readings set years in advance, so Roman-rite parishes in Manila and in Munich hear the same Gospel on the same Sunday. Israel and the church are one people of God across both Testaments. And on the gifts of the Holy Spirit the sketch leans continuationist, which startles Protestants: Lumen Gentium says the Spirit hands out special graces among the faithful of every rank, and charismatic renewal has been at home in Catholic parishes since 1967.

did_you_know.text: Catholic does not mean Latin. The church is made of twenty-four self-governing churches: the Latin one most Westerners picture, and twenty-three Eastern Catholic churches with their own liturgies, their own canon law and, in many of them, married priests, all in full communion with the pope.
did_you_know.source: 24 sui iuris churches: the Latin Church and 23 Eastern Catholic Churches.

did_you_know.text: The council blamed for abolishing Latin did not abolish it. Sacrosanctum Concilium opens its article on language by saying the use of Latin is to be preserved in the Latin rites, then permits wider use of the local tongue. The bishops’ conferences took that permission a great deal further than the text expected.
did_you_know.source: Sacrosanctum Concilium 36 (1963).

catholic-roman-and-eastern.family: Catholics trace their communion to the apostles without a break, and historically the Western church is the parent of nearly everything else on this map. East and West broke communion in 1054; the Protestants left in the sixteenth century. The nearest relative here is the Eastern Orthodox church, which shares the sacraments, the liturgy and much of the reading of grace, and differs about the pope and about how doctrine may develop. Anglicans and confessional Lutherans stand next, each having kept more of the old shape than they usually get credit for.

read.placed_from: Catechism 1996-2001, 1257, 1374-1376; Trent Sess. VI ch. 5 and can. 4, Sess. XIII can. 1; Lumen Gentium 12; Dei Verbum 9-10; Sacrosanctum Concilium 22 and 102.

open.title: The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992)
open.note: Free online and numbered by paragraph, so a reference lands you exactly where it says. 1996 to 2001 is grace; 1374 to 1376 the Eucharist.

open.title: Dei Verbum (1965)
open.note: Vatican II on where revelation comes from. Six short chapters, and section 9 is the one Protestants and Catholics argue over.

charismatic-non-denominational.in_a_sentence: Independent churches, often with no denominational name at all, that expect the Holy Spirit to speak and heal today. Services are built around sung worship and praying for people.
what_marks_it_out: Everything begins with the gifts. These churches hold that every gift Paul lists is still given: prophecy, healing, words of knowledge, and tongues, which means praying in a language the speaker has never learned.

What separates them from Pentecostals is one sentence they decline to say. Classical Pentecostals teach that speaking in tongues is the first physical evidence that someone has been baptised in the Holy Spirit. Charismatics of this kind treat tongues as one gift among many, given to some and not to others, which is what Paul’s own run of questions in 1 Corinthians 12 expects.

On Israel and the church the map names nothing, and the silence is accurate: these churches rarely take a side on prophecy charts at all. What they did absorb is George Eldon Ladd’s reading of the kingdom of God as already begun and not yet finished. John Wimber turned that into a reason to pray for a sick person right now. If the kingdom has genuinely broken in, some of its effects should be visible before the end.

On grace the sketch leans to the cooperating side: God’s grace comes first and makes faith possible, and each person must answer and may decline. On authority the Bible stands alone, with no confession, bishop or synod above it. That combination is what makes a church like this quick to plant and hard to generalise about, because there is usually no document you can read to find out what the one down your road actually teaches.

A service is long on singing and short on ceremony: a band, a stretch of worship, a sermon from an open Bible, and time at the end when people come forward and are prayed for by name. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance, taken as often as the church decides. Nothing about the room says what century you are in.

did_you_know.text: The movement got its name in a seminary classroom. C. Peter Wagner called it the third wave of the Holy Spirit, after Pentecostalism and after the charismatic renewal inside the older denominations, while he and John Wimber were teaching a Fuller Seminary course called Signs and Wonders in 1983.
did_you_know.source: C. Peter Wagner’s term “Third Wave”, popularised around the 1983 Fuller course MC510, Signs and Wonders, taught with John Wimber.

did_you_know.text: The Vineyard, the best known network of this kind, was recognised as an association in 1982, and it came out of Calvary Chapel rather than out of Pentecostalism. John Wimber’s church in Yorba Linda separated that year over how freely the gifts should be used on a Sunday morning.
did_you_know.source: Association of Vineyard Churches recognised 1982; Calvary Chapel Yorba Linda became Anaheim Vineyard under John Wimber.

charismatic-non-denominational.family: A wing of the twentieth century’s Pentecostal awakening rather than a denomination. Pentecostalism came first, from Azusa Street in Los Angeles in 1906. The charismatic renewal followed in the 1960s, inside Anglican, Catholic and mainline parishes that stayed where they were. This third group came later still and mostly outside all of them: the Vineyard, and thousands of single congregations with one-word names and no denominational tie at all. Its nearest relatives here are the Pentecostals and Calvary Chapel.

read.placed_from: Vineyard USA Statement of Faith; Ladd, A Theology of the New Testament (the inaugurated kingdom Vineyard teaches); Third Wave practice.

open.title: The Vineyard USA Statement of Faith
open.note: Short and online. The sections on the Holy Spirit and on the kingdom are where this tradition parts from Pentecostalism.

open.title: George Eldon Ladd, A Theology of the New Testament
open.note: Not a charismatic book at all, but the source of the already-and-not-yet kingdom these churches pray out of.

churches-of-christ-christian-churches.in_a_sentence: Churches that set out to be simply Christians, with no denominational name and no creed but the New Testament. They baptise believers by immersion for the forgiveness of sins.
what_marks_it_out: Baptism is where this tradition parts company with most of evangelical America. Acts 2:38 reads: “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins.” These churches take that ‘for’ at face value. Immersion is the moment a believer is saved, not a sign that he already was, and they insist it is nothing he performs: it is being buried with Christ and raised with Him.

The rule behind almost everything else is Thomas Campbell’s: where the Scriptures speak, we speak; where the Scriptures are silent, we are silent. Applied strictly it takes a great deal out. No bishops, no synods, no denominational headquarters, no creed beyond the confession that Jesus is the Christ. In the a cappella congregations it takes out the instruments too, since the New Testament mentions Christians singing and never mentions them playing.

On communion the map names no position, and the reason is genuinely odd. These churches take the Lord’s Supper every single Sunday, more faithfully than most sacramental churches manage, and yet describe it as a memorial of Christ’s death rather than a change in the bread. The frequency points one way and the definition points the other, so the rail stays in the middle.

On grace they sit as far from Calvinism as this map goes. A person hears, believes, repents, confesses and is baptised, and none of it happens to him without him. On the gifts they are firmly cessationist, holding that tongues and prophecy belonged to the years before the New Testament was finished and were withdrawn once it was. Worship is plain, the sermon is the centre, and in an a cappella congregation the singing is the whole room and nothing else.

did_you_know.text: A census split the movement in two. Disagreement over instruments in worship and over missionary societies had been growing for decades, and in 1906 the United States Bureau of the Census listed Churches of Christ and Disciples of Christ as separate bodies for the first time. The paperwork made official a division that had already happened.
did_you_know.source: 1906 US Census of Religious Bodies listed Churches of Christ separately from the Disciples; the split turned on instrumental music and missionary societies.

did_you_know.text: One of its two founders came out of the largest revival on the American frontier. Barton W. Stone was a Presbyterian minister at the Cane Ridge camp meeting in Kentucky in 1801, where thousands camped for days. He left the Presbyterians soon after, and in 1832 his people and Alexander Campbell’s joined forces.
did_you_know.source: Cane Ridge revival, Kentucky, 1801; the Stone and Campbell movements united in 1832.

churches-of-christ-christian-churches.family: The Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement, an American original born on the frontier in the early 1800s out of sheer exhaustion with denominational quarrelling. Three bodies came out of it: the a cappella Churches of Christ, the instrumental Christian Churches and Churches of Christ, and the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), which went in a mainline direction. This page covers the first two. Baptists are the nearest relatives in practice, and the long family argument with them is almost entirely about what baptism does.

read.placed_from: Alexander Campbell, The Christian System; the Acts 2:38 and Acts 2:47 teaching on baptism and on the church begun at Pentecost; "no creed but Christ".

open.title: Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
open.note: The founding document, thirteen propositions long. The first of them: the Church of Christ upon earth is essentially, intentionally, and constitutionally one.

open.title: Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839)
open.note: The movement’s theology laid out in full by its ablest debater, and still the best single source for why it does what it does.

eastern-orthodox.in_a_sentence: The churches of the Christian East, in communion with one another but not with Rome, and led by patriarchs rather than a pope. Their worship has changed remarkably little since the first millennium.
what_marks_it_out: Orthodoxy is a liturgy before it is a theology, and Orthodox writers say so first. The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom is sung on most Sundays of the year from a fixed text, almost always unaccompanied, in a church covered with icons. Very little is chosen by the priest and nothing is projected on a screen. If you want to know what Orthodox Christians believe, the usual advice from inside is to come and stand through it.

The East’s word for how salvation works is synergy, from the Greek for working together, and it is not a compromise between two Western options: it predates the argument entirely. God’s grace does everything, and the person must genuinely cooperate with it. Behind that stands a larger claim called theosis, that salvation is not only forgiveness but real participation in the life of God. Athanasius put it in the fourth century: God became man so that man might become god, which means becoming by grace what God is by nature, not sharing His essence.

Scripture belongs to the church that produced it, and is read alongside the councils, the liturgy and the Fathers rather than against them. There are seven ecumenical councils; the seventh, at Nicaea in 787, settled that icons may be venerated, on the argument that God Himself took a body that could be painted. The Eucharist is the body and blood of Christ, and the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672 was willing to use a Greek word equivalent to transubstantiation while insisting that the how of it stays a mystery.

On the gifts of the Holy Spirit the sketch leans continuationist, because nothing in this tradition ever announced that God had stopped. Healings, miracles and holy people who see what others cannot are part of its ordinary expectation rather than a special movement within it.

did_you_know.text: The Great Schism has an end date almost nobody knows. The mutual excommunications of 1054 were lifted on 7 December 1965, when a joint declaration by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I was read out at the same hour in Rome and in Istanbul, committing the sentences to oblivion. The two churches are still not in communion. The anathemas are gone.
did_you_know.source: Catholic-Orthodox Joint Declaration of Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I, 7 December 1965.

did_you_know.text: Orthodox babies receive communion. Baptism, chrismation (the anointing that became confirmation in the West) and first communion all happen at the same service whatever the age of the person baptised, and an infant is carried to the chalice every Sunday after that. The West did the same until about the twelfth century.
did_you_know.source: Eastern Orthodox practice; the Latin Church discontinued infant communion around the twelfth century.

did_you_know.text: The longer Liturgy of St Basil the Great is used exactly ten times a year: the five Sundays of Great Lent, Holy Thursday, Holy Saturday, the eves of Christmas and Theophany, and 1 January, which is St Basil’s own feast.
did_you_know.source: Byzantine rite: the Liturgy of St Basil is appointed ten times a year.

eastern-orthodox.family: One half of the undivided church of the first thousand years. East and West drifted apart over centuries and broke communion in 1054, over the pope’s authority and over the filioque, a clause the West added to the Nicene Creed saying the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father. Orthodoxy today is a communion of self-governing churches, Greek, Russian, Serbian, Romanian, Antiochian and more, with the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople first in honour rather than in command. The Oriental Orthodox churches, which parted earlier still, are a separate communion.

read.placed_from: Synod of Jerusalem (1672), Decrees 3 and 15-17; John of Damascus, On the Orthodox Faith IV.9 and IV.13; the Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom; Seventh Ecumenical Council.

open.title: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
open.note: The text itself, online in full. Reading it straight through is the fastest way to meet Orthodoxy from the inside.

open.title: John of Damascus, An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
open.note: Eighth century, and still the standard summary. Book IV, chapters 9 and 13, are baptism and the Eucharist.

lutheran-confessional.in_a_sentence: Lutheran churches that still bind themselves word for word to the Book of Concord of 1580, keeping a liturgy that looks Catholic from the outside. Salvation here is entirely God’s work.
what_marks_it_out: Lutherans teach that a person contributes nothing whatever to his own conversion. The Holy Spirit works faith through the preached Word and the sacraments, and the will before that is not neutral but dead. That is monergism, the view that God alone brings a person to believe, and on this axis it ought to put Lutherans at the very end of the rail.

It does not, because they refuse the second half of the Reformed package: they will not say grace cannot finally be resisted, and they will not say God chose anyone for damnation. If a person is saved it is all God; if a person is lost it is all his own doing. The Formula of Concord leaves that asymmetry standing instead of tidying it away, so an honest confessional Lutheran lands just short of the post.

On communion Lutherans are as sacramental as anyone on this map. The body and blood of Christ are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. They reject the word consubstantiation, which their opponents coined for them, because it sounds like two substances mixed and because it sounds like an explanation. They do not think the how can be explained. “This is My body” is taken to be enough.

And yet Scripture alone. The Formula of Concord calls Scripture the only rule and norm by which every teaching and every teacher must be judged. The creeds and the confessions are kept and subscribed because they are held to say exactly what Scripture says, not because they stand beside it as a second authority.

Worship keeps the historic shape of the Mass, with confession, Kyrie, Gloria, creed and the words of institution in their old places, under a church year beginning in Advent. On the last things, Augsburg Confession XVII condemns the idea that before the resurrection the godly will take possession of an earthly kingdom, which rules out the entire dispensational scheme in a sentence written in 1530. On the gifts, confessional Lutherans do not practise tongues or prophecy: Augsburg Confession V insists the Holy Spirit comes through the Word and the sacraments and not apart from them.

did_you_know.text: Luther wrote the Small Catechism because of what he saw on an inspection tour. Sent round the Saxon parishes in 1528, he found that ordinary people could not say the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed or the Ten Commandments, and that many of their pastors could not teach them. His preface calls it a deplorable, wretched deprivation. The little book he wrote the next year is still learned by heart.
did_you_know.source: Luther, Preface to the Small Catechism (1529), on the Saxon visitation of 1528.

did_you_know.text: The Augsburg Confession was read aloud to an emperor. On 25 June 1530 the Lutheran princes had it read out in German before Charles V at the imperial diet in Augsburg, as their answer to the charge of heresy. It is still the document a confessional Lutheran pastor subscribes.
did_you_know.source: Augsburg Confession presented to Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg, 25 June 1530.

lutheran-confessional.family: The first Protestants, and for a while the only ones. Lutheranism starts with Martin Luther’s protest of 1517 and takes fixed form in the Book of Concord of 1580, which gathers the three ancient creeds, the Augsburg Confession, Luther’s two catechisms and the Formula of Concord into one volume. Confessional in the name means a church body that still subscribes to all of it, chiefly the Lutheran Church Missouri Synod and the Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod in North America. The larger, looser Lutheran bodies appear on this map under mainline Protestant.

read.placed_from: Formula of Concord, Preface ("the only rule and norm") and Epitome II and XI; Augsburg Confession IX, X, XVII; Small Catechism IV; the Divine Service.

open.title: The Augsburg Confession (1530)
open.note: Twenty-eight short articles and the clearest statement of what Lutherans think they are. IX is baptism, X the Supper, XVII the last day.

open.title: Luther’s Small Catechism (1529)
open.note: Six parts and a few pages, written for a father to teach his household at the table. Every commandment answered with: what does this mean?
